recordings.text: Spicy geometry: the piece that just landed forks a whole cluster of targets, and they can rarely all dodge in one turn.
Eyes up: a fork is loading for the other side, one of their pieces about to land among several targets at once.
Tucked inside another move was a fork, one jump onto a cluster of targets. That punchline stays in the drawer here.
Snap: that front piece can't budge without exposing its king to check. Nailed down.
Psst, the other side can nail a piece to its king now, and a piece stuck like that can't wander off the line.
The stronger move had a pin against the king up its sleeve, nailing a piece in place. Here the piece goes free.
Skewer, and a spicy one. Poke the big piece in front, and when it hops aside, the one hiding behind is left to the wolves.
Little detail with big teeth: a skewer is lining up for the other side, front piece chased off and the one behind left open.
The stronger move had a skewer tucked away, front piece chased, back piece exposed. A spicy one to set up and replay.
Punchline: the bodyguard gets captured, and whatever it was shielding is suddenly up for grabs.
Freeze frame: the other side can capture a bodyguard now, and whatever it shields could tumble right after.
The stronger move would have captured a bodyguard and left its client exposed. That trapdoor stays shut.
Back-rank tripwire. The king's own pieces crowd its home row, so the mating net is set on that row.
Eyes up on the home row: the other side has a mating tripwire there, with the king crowded in by its own pieces.
The back-rank tripwire was armed, the king crowded in by its own pieces. This move never trips it.
Sizzle: a pawn sprinting to the promotion row to turn into a brand-new piece. Count the squares of that sprint.
Psst, one of the other side's pawns is gearing up for a promotion sprint. Count the squares it still needs.
The stronger move set a pawn sprinting for the promotion row. Here that sprint never leaves the blocks.
Slingshot: the front piece zips out of the way, and the piece hiding behind it opens fire.
Eyes up: the other side has a slingshot ready, one piece zipping aside so the one behind can fire.
The stronger move had a slingshot loaded, the front piece zipping aside so its partner could fire. Never launched.
Two threats juggled in one go, and that's the punchline. A single reply may not cover both.
Eyes up: the other side gets a double act, one move juggling two threats. Spot both before replying.
The stronger move had two threats ready to juggle. This one never stages that double act.
Decoy: the defender takes the bait, and its real job goes begging.
Decoy alert: the other side can tempt a defender off its post, and whatever it watches over might come loose.
A decoy was available in the stronger move, luring a defender off its post. Here it gets to stay comfy.
Free snack: that piece had no lookout, and this capture gobbles it up.
Another move could have gobbled a piece nobody was watching, and this one leaves the snack on the table. Always scan for freebies.
Little detail: one piece has zero lookouts, and the other side can simply gobble it.
Here's the leak. This move walks away from the only real bodyguard a piece had, and the other side can collect what's left.
The opponent's last move had teeth, and this move shrugs it off. That leaves a piece dangling.
One capture down, one to go: the recapture bites something heavier, so the trade goes sour.
A knight or bishop pops off its home square and joins the party.
Another move gets a knight or bishop out to play; this one keeps them home.
The rook gets a highway: zero pawns of either color on its file.
A different move would have put a rook on a pawnless highway of a file.
Half a highway for the rook: no friendly pawn on the file, an enemy pawn parked further up.
A different move would have handed a rook half a highway, only enemy pawns parked on the file.
Passed pawn alert. Nothing enemy-pawn-shaped stands in front of it on its own file or the two files hugging it.
A different move would have minted a passed pawn, nothing enemy-pawn-shaped ahead of it on its file or the files hugging it.
The passed pawn inches up again. Closer and closer.
Another move gets the passer one notch nearer the promotion row.
A pawn ends up stranded, isolated, with no friendly pawn on the files at its elbows.
A different move would have stranded a pawn, isolated with no friendly pawn at its elbows.
A piece that was flapping in the wind gets a bodyguard. One loose end fewer.
A different move would have hired a bodyguard for an unguarded piece.
Little detail: a piece is now flapping in the wind, no defender at all. That alone doesn't mean it's winnable.
A different move would have left a piece flapping in the wind, though that alone wouldn't make it winnable.
The king gets a fresh escape hatch, a legal square that wasn't open before.
A different move would have cut a fresh escape hatch for the king.
Castling: king tucked into the corner side, rook hopping over beside it, all in one move.
The other option was castling, the king tucked away and the rook hopping across together.
This capture breaks up the bishop duo, so that side has bishops on just one color now.
A different move would have snagged one of the other side's bishops, breaking up its duo.
Doubled pawns: a same-colored pair now queues on one file.
A different move would have doubled pawns, a same-colored pair queuing up.
Freeze frame. This opens a forced mate, so let's watch exactly how the attack crashes through.
Mate by force was right there, and this move lets it slip through the fingers. Rewind and hunt down that finish.
Sacrifice, and it stands its ground. Grab the material in the line we checked, and the idea keeps sizzling anyway.
The one rope that held. Every other move we checked sank; this alone kept things afloat.
Out of every move we checked, only this kept the edge alive; the rest all let it go and lost.
Eyes up: something can be gobbled by the other side at once. Before anything else, that reply goes on the board.
Spicy reply: the sharpest answer checks, so the king gets the first say.

Castling mates. Sneaky geometry, and the other king is out of options.
One landing forks a cluster of targets, and one of them gets collected. When the dust settles, that side is up material.
Capturing is off the menu for that piece: it's nailed to its king, and stepping off would hand that king a check.
The attacked piece is nailed to its king, so fleeing is off the table. Anything it does has to keep its king screened.
Every defender is nailed to its king, which rules out recapturing. Hence the capture sticks, and the line shown ends up material ahead.
Keep tabs on the pinned piece. Stepping off the line would bare its king, so it gets gobbled as the line plays out.
